sources.title: F. Scott Fitzgerald (Q93354) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-16): English label 'F. Scott Fitzgerald', description 'American writer (1896-1940)', born 24 September 1896, died 21 December 1940, citizenship United States of America, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'F. Scott Fitzgerald' (article by the biographer Arthur Mizener, fact-checked by Britannica's editors; page last updated 20 September 2026) -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: encyclopaedia biography calling him a 20th-century American short-story writer and novelist, a key figure of the Lost Generation and famous for his depictions of the Jazz Age, who completed four novels and more than 150 short stories; says The Great Gatsby (1925) is today widely considered the great American novel, that This Side of Paradise (1920) was a revelation of the new morality of the young and made him famous (fame opened literary magazines such as Scribner's and high-paying popular ones such as the Saturday Evening Post), that some of his finest stories, including 'The Rich Boy' and 'Absolution', appeared in All the Sad Young Men (1926), that Tender Is the Night (1934) was commercially unsuccessful, and that he became a Hollywood scriptwriter in 1937 and began The Last Tycoon in October 1939. Admiring and retrospective (Mizener was a Fitzgerald biographer); its passages on his marriage, drinking, health and death were read and not used. Read in full.

Princeton University Library, 'Digitization of The Great Gatsby Autograph Manuscript and Galleys', PUL Manuscripts News, 24 May 2013 (the same announcement by the curator Don Skemer also ran in Princeton University's news archive) -- curators' account of the F. Scott Fitzgerald Papers: a first Gatsby ('Ur-Gatsby') planned from June 1922 and written in 1923 (some 18,000 words, set in the Midwest around 1885, no Nick Carraway as narrator), taken up again in April 1924 in a 1922 setting, the manuscript finished in France by September 1924, the typescript sent to Maxwell Perkins in November 1924, the 'Trimalchio' galleys revised in Rome in the first two months of 1925 in pencil and with long pasted typed additions (James L. W. West III: not the same novel as the published book), corrections and alternative titles sent to Perkins by letter and telegram, publication on 10 April 1925 under the title Perkins liked best, and a personal first-edition copy he corrected for later printings. Institutional and built on Matthew Bruccoli's scholarship; the post gives the span of the work as both three and four years and the manuscript as both 302 pages and just over 250, so no duration or page count is used. Read in full.

University of South Carolina Libraries (Thomas Cooper Library), Matthew and Arlyn Bruccoli Collection of F. Scott Fitzgerald, 'Life of Fitzgerald' -- institutional biography from the university's Fitzgerald collection: a first novel rejected by Scribner's with praise for its originality and a request to resubmit when revised, rejected again after revision, rewritten in St. Paul in 1919 as This Side of Paradise and accepted by Maxwell Perkins; from autumn 1919 popular stories for mass-circulation magazines through the agent Harold Ober, the Saturday Evening Post his best market, a peak Post fee of $4,000 and some 160 magazine stories; the failed 1923 tryout of his play The Vegetable; the statement that he was a painstaking reviser whose fiction went through layers of drafts although critics were reluctant to credit him as a serious craftsman; Gatsby as a striking advance in technique with disappointing sales; little progress on a fourth novel in the late 1920s; unsuccessful Hollywood stints in 1927 and 1931; the 1937 MGM contract at $1,000 a week, the only screen credit (Three Comrades) and a renewal at $1,250; freelance scripts and short pieces for Esquire after MGM dropped its option; and The Love of the Last Tycoon begun in 1939 with more than half a working draft written. Admiring (the collection is Bruccoli's); its many passages on his marriage, drinking and health were read and not used. Read in full.

University of South Carolina Libraries, 'The Warner Bros./Turner Entertainment F. Scott Fitzgerald Screenplay Collection' -- the library's description of the roughly 2,000-page MGM archive it acquired in 2004 (manuscripts, revised typescripts and working drafts for Three Comrades, Infidelity and The Women, 1937-39): the July 1937 six-month contract at $1,000 a week; his September 1937 request to work alone on the Three Comrades revisions and producer Joseph Mankiewicz's reply that the pages were 'simply swell'; the assignment of E. E. Paramore as collaborator and Fitzgerald's October 1937 letter saying he preferred to keep responsibility for the script as a whole; six revisions between November 1937 and February 1938; Mankiewicz's heavy final revision and Fitzgerald's note in his shooting script that the shadows and rhythm of his pages were removed; the Infidelity assignment for Joan Crawford, whose films he studied, and his June 1938 letter about inventing and rejecting solutions; The Women; and Budd Schulberg's testimony to his determination to develop his screenwriting. Library acquisition page, so promotional and admiring, and the studio's side appears only in outline. Read in full.

'The Literary Spotlight, VI: F. Scott Fitzgerald', The Bookman (New York), March 1922, with a caricature by William Gropper, Internet Archive scan of the issue -- CONTEMPORARY CRITIC, unsigned in the magazine and attributed to Edmund Wilson, a Princeton friend, by later scholarship that was not opened; written when Fitzgerald was 25: calls This Side of Paradise highly imitative yet alive and well written, credits an instinct for graceful and vivid prose while saying he plays the language by ear and misuses words, judges his imagination to lack intellectual control, discipline and aesthetic ideas, reports that he moved to the 'ironical-pessimistic' school of fiction and that the first version of The Beautiful and Damned ended in arbitrary catastrophes, and tells how he laughed at one such passage and improvised a burlesque when others did. Friendly but openly critical; its remarks on ethnic character and personality were not used, and the last sentence is cut at a page break in the scan. Read in full.

CBS News, 'How F. Scott Fitzgerald's Saturday Evening Post success helped "Gatsby" vision come to life' (Jeff Glor and Alvin Patrick, 7 May 2013, written to accompany a film release) -- news report built on the Post's archivist Jeff Nilsson, who says Fitzgerald wrote 68 stories for the Post over 17 years, that his fee rose from $400 in 1920 to $4,000 by 1929, that the stories began as humorous, romantic commercial pieces and took on more modernist tones over time, that Hemingway taunted him that the Post would be the graveyard of his talent, and that Fitzgerald said late in his career that he never compromised or went for a cheap formula. Press item with a commercial interest in the Post's reputation; Hemingway and Fitzgerald are quoted only as relayed by the archivist, and the report's $2 million total and its remarks on his courtship and spending were not used. Read in full.

Library of America, Story of the Week, 'Head and Shoulders' (18 September 2015) -- editorial note on Fitzgerald's first story for the Saturday Evening Post: his agent Harold Ober sold 'Head and Shoulders' (first submitted as 'Nest Feathers') to the Post for $400, three times what the magazine Smart Set had paid him, and the note quotes Matthew Bruccoli on the pressure he would be under to provide literary entertainment. Short editorial note by a literary publisher; its passages on his engagement and marriage were not used. Read in full.

Open Yale Courses, AMST 246 'Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Faulkner', Lecture 4, 'Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby' (Professor Wai Chee Dimock; lecture transcript) -- university lecture that quotes Maxwell Perkins's letter of 20 November 1924 asking that Gatsby be described more distinctly and calling him vague, and Fitzgerald's reply of 20 December 1924, and reads Fitzgerald as deliberate and stubborn in not giving in to Perkins's suggestion; it also reads the novel as experimental counter-realism. One modern lecturer's interpretation; the primary letters were not opened and the quoted wording is the transcript's. Read the opening sections on Perkins and the novel's experimentalism in full; the rest of the lecture (literary analysis of the text) was skimmed and not used.

University of South Carolina Press, publisher's page for 'Trimalchio: A Facsimile Edition of the Original Galley Proofs for The Great Gatsby' (2000, edited with an afterword by Matthew Bruccoli) -- says the book reproduces the only extant set of the unrevised galleys, that in the four months after sending the typescript to Maxwell Perkins Fitzgerald extensively revised and rewrote the text in galley proof, that his winter 1924-25 work included substantial rewriting and reordering of chapters 6, 7 and 8, and that the novel met warm reviews but disappointing sales. Short publisher's page, promotional; its statement that he chose a new title at Perkins's urging differs from Princeton's account and was not used. Read in full.

The World's Work (Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page), volume 42, June 1921, page 192, in the feature on authors and best sellers -- Internet Archive scan from the University of Toronto's Robarts Library; the text layer carries an item headed 'Scott Fitzgerald' (index entry 'Fitzgerald, Scott 192') on the page where the portrait photograph was printed, with no photographer credit, and the Internet Archive item carries no rights or licence statement. Opened to check the portrait's first publication; not used for any scoring.

Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, '[Portrait of F. Scott Fitzgerald]' by Carl Van Vechten, gelatin silver print dated 4 June 1937 (LCCN 2004662885, reproduction number LC-USZ62-88103), with the Division's rights statement for the Carl Van Vechten Photographs (last revised 7 May 2024) -- opened to check the alternative portrait: the Library 'continues to believe' the photographs are in the public domain after the donor's restrictions expired in 1986, but records that the Van Vechten trustee asks that photographs not be cropped or colorized and that the photographer be credited, notes a dispute over the donor's executor's authority, and warns that privacy and publicity rights may apply. Not used; see the portrait notes.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby, src_fitzgerald_uscpress_trimalchio, src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays, src_fitzgerald_wilson1922 | 1922-1938 | university-library curators + university press + university-library biography + library page on the MGM archive + contemporary critic] Princeton's curators describe corrections on nearly every page of the Gatsby manuscript, galleys revised in the first two months of 1925 in pencil and with long pasted typed additions (citing James L. W. West III that the galley text was not the same novel as the published one), his hesitation over the title and a personal copy of the first edition that he corrected for later printings; the University of South Carolina Press says he extensively revised and rewrote the text in galley proof, with substantial rewriting and reordering of chapters 6 to 8; the University of South Carolina Libraries call him a painstaking reviser whose fiction went through layers of drafts and list six revisions of the Three Comrades script and heavily revised drafts of Infidelity, on which he wrote that he had spent a month thinking about the project, inventing and rejecting solutions. Several documented episodes across a novel and film scripts, but every institutional source draws on one scholarly lineage (Matthew Bruccoli), the same biography notes that critics were reluctant to credit him as a serious craftsman, and the 1922 Bookman essay judged his imagination to lack discipline, so a real but moderate lean at moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72/0.58 to 64/0.50 (single-lineage concentration in Bruccoli-derived sources; interpretation stronger than behaviour, since heavy revision is common among novelists and no source reports an inability to finish or let go of a draft).

persistence.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby, src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays, src_fitzgerald_britannica | 1917-1939 | university-library biography + university-library curators + library page on the MGM archive + encyclopaedia biography] The USC Libraries biography says his first novel was rejected by Scribner's, rejected again after revision, and that he quit his job in July 1919 to rewrite it as This Side of Paradise, which Perkins accepted in September; Princeton's curators say he abandoned a first attempt at Gatsby of some 18,000 words, took the book up again in April 1924 in a new setting and finished the manuscript by September 1924; the biography records two unsuccessful Hollywood stints (one before spring 1927 and one in 1931) before the 1937 MGM contract that brought a credit on Three Comrades and a renewal (the MGM page agrees), and says he freelanced after MGM dropped its option and began The Last Tycoon in 1939 with more than half of a working draft written, a start Britannica dates to October 1939. The same biography notes little progress on a fourth novel through the late 1920s, so persistence was uneven across projects. Four documented episodes across two decades, but the early rejections and the two earlier Hollywood failures rest on one biography. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68/0.56 to 64/0.52 (single-biographer dependence for the rejections and the earlier Hollywood stints; Princeton, the MGM page and Britannica corroborate only the Gatsby restart, the MGM credit and the Tycoon start).

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays, src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby | 1927-1938 | library page on the MGM archive + university-library biography + university-library curators] The MGM archive page quotes the screenwriter Budd Schulberg, his last collaborator on a film assignment, on Fitzgerald's determination to develop his screenwriting skills and his regard for film as an art form deserving as serious attention as his novels and plays, and records that for the Joan Crawford assignment he studied her films to tailor the role to her abilities and that his time on Three Comrades was logged in his own manuscript record; the biography records two unsuccessful Hollywood trips before the third produced a screen credit; Princeton notes that he went on marking changes in a personal copy of Gatsby after publication. Learning a new craft after earlier failures is specific behaviour, but the main witness is one admiring collaborator quoted on a page written to promote a library acquisition, and Mankiewicz's heavy rewriting of the final script shows the results were limited. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68/0.54 to 62/0.48 and relabelled inference (admiring-source concentration: Schulberg's testimony and the 'seriousness' framing come from an acquisition page; interpretation stronger than behaviour).

experimentation.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_wilson1922, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby, src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_yale_dimock | 1922-1925 | contemporary critic + university-library curators + university-library biography + university lecturer] The 1922 Bookman essay says that after This Side of Paradise he took up the ironical-pessimistic school of fiction and that the first version of The Beautiful and Damned ended in a run of catastrophes the critic thought arbitrary; Princeton's curators describe a first Gatsby set in the Midwest around 1885 with no Nick Carraway as narrator that he discarded for a version set in 1922; the USC biography records a stage play, The Vegetable, that failed at its 1923 tryout, and says Gatsby used a complex structure and a controlled narrative point of view; Yale's Wai Chee Dimock reads the novel as experimental counter-realism. Several documented changes of form and approach, but some did not succeed, the experimental reading is a later lecturer's and the first is a single contemporary account. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66/0.54 to 62/0.50 (interpretation stronger than behaviour; retrospective reading).

creative_originality.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_britannica, src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_wilson1922, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby | 1917-1925 | encyclopaedia biography + university-library biography + contemporary critic + university-library curators] Britannica (Arthur Mizener) calls This Side of Paradise a revelation of the new morality of the young and Gatsby the most profoundly American novel of its time; the USC biography says Scribner's first rejection praised his first novel's originality, that his early stories introduced a fresh character (the independent, determined young American woman) and that Gatsby marked a striking advance in technique; Princeton shows him discarding a first conception set in the Midwest around 1885 for one set in 1922. Against that, the 1922 Bookman essay called This Side of Paradise highly imitative and drawn from a bad model while granting a brilliant imagination whose next product could not be predicted. The praise is largely retrospective and from admiring biographers, and the one contemporary independent critic disputed the early originality, so inference-level at modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68/0.48 to 62/0.44 (retrospective praise; a contemporary critic's contrary view).

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_wilson1922, src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_britannica, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby | 1922-1939 | contemporary critic + university-library biography + encyclopaedia biography + university-library curators] The 1922 Bookman essay credits him with an instinct for graceful and vivid prose which some more serious writers might envy, while saying he plays the language by ear, misuses words and has a desire for beauty without an aesthetic ideal; the USC biography calls his style clear, lyrical, colorful and witty, evoking the emotions of time and place; Britannica's Mizener praises the brilliance of expression of the late Hollywood novel; Princeton shows word-level corrections on nearly every page of the Gatsby manuscript and a long search for a title. A real concern with the sound and look of language is described from several angles, but most of the praise is retrospective and the contemporary critic found the sensitivity unguided, so a moderate lean at moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72/0.54 to 66/0.50 (retrospective praise from admiring biographers; evidence of style more than of sensitivity).

belief_updating.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_wilson1922, src_fitzgerald_princeton_gatsby, src_fitzgerald_uscpress_trimalchio, src_fitzgerald_yale_dimock, src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays | 1917-1938 | university-library biography + contemporary critic + university-library curators + university press + university lecturer + library page on the MGM archive] The USC biography says Scribner's first rejection of his first novel asked that it be resubmitted when revised, and that it was revised and rejected again before the 1919 rewrite; the 1922 essay reports that when others laughed at a catastrophic passage in the first version of The Beautiful and Damned he laughed at it himself and improvised a burlesque; Princeton and the University of South Carolina Press show Gatsby extensively rewritten in galley proof after the typescript went to Perkins. Against that, Wai Chee Dimock reads his reply to Perkins's criticism of Gatsby's vagueness (Perkins's letter is dated 20 November 1924 and the reply 20 December 1924) as deliberate and stubborn, and the MGM page shows him resisting a collaborator's role. Responsive to criticism in revision, firm where he judged the conception central; the evidence cuts both ways, one anecdote comes from a critic's account and the letters are known only through a lecture, so mid-range with a dual-edged impact at modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): not lowered; scored conservatively at the outset because the evidence points both ways and no single episode carries the row.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays, src_fitzgerald_yale_dimock | 1924-1938 | library page on the MGM archive + university lecturer] The MGM archive page records that on 4 September 1937 Fitzgerald asked the producer Joseph Mankiewicz to let him work alone on the Three Comrades revisions and Mankiewicz agreed, calling the submitted pages 'simply swell'; that after the studio assigned E. E. Paramore as collaborator, who saw himself as an equal partner, Fitzgerald wrote on 24 October that he preferred to keep responsibility for the script as a whole; that he resented Mankiewicz's later interference; and that in early 1938 he was assigned to write Infidelity alone; Wai Chee Dimock reads his December 1924 reply to his editor as holding to his own conception of Gatsby. Two documented episodes in film and a scholar's reading of one in fiction, but both film episodes come from one library page that gives Fitzgerald's side far more fully than the studio's, and the assignment of a collaborator was the studio's decision, so inference-level at modest confidence with a dual-edged impact. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64/0.50 to 60/0.46 and relabelled inference (single-source dependence; Fitzgerald's own words relayed through one page).

adaptability.rationale: [src_fitzgerald_usc_life, src_fitzgerald_loa_head, src_fitzgerald_cbs_post, src_fitzgerald_usc_screenplays | 1919-1939 | university-library biography + literary-publisher note + news report quoting the Post's archivist + library page on the MGM archive] The USC biography says that from autumn 1919 he wrote popular stories for mass-circulation magazines through the agent Harold Ober, with the Saturday Evening Post his best market, and went on interrupting his novels to do so for the rest of his life; the Library of America puts the fee for his first Post story at $400 and CBS News reports the Post's archivist saying it reached $4,000 by 1929 and that the stories moved from humorous commercial pieces toward more modernist tones over time; the MGM page shows him studying Joan Crawford's films to tailor a screenplay to her abilities and working through six revisions with an assigned collaborator, and the biography adds that after MGM dropped its option he freelanced scripts and wrote short-short stories for Esquire. Writing for several markets and for a studio is documented, but the sources do not describe how he adjusted, he resented the studio's changes, and the Post material comes from a promotional news report. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62/0.48 to 58/0.44 (interpretation stronger than behaviour; the Post pattern rests on one news report and one biography).

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT (done before deep reading): QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-16) for Q93354 returned en label 'F. Scott Fitzgerald', description 'American writer (1896-1940)', born 1896-09-24, died 1940-12-21, instance of human, citizenship United States, ko label 'F. 스콧 피츠제럴드'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no existing candidate file, production roster entry or QID collision in the roster51 worktree for slug f-scott-fitzgerald or Q93354 (only a passing mention of Fitzgerald in Hemingway's profile text and in a coverage note). Region north_america valid; era 20th_century (Hemingway and Joyce are the precedents). Vocabulary: occupation writer, field literature, impact domains literary and cultural, tag prolific and archetype creative_creator are existing ids used by Hemingway, Goethe, Melville and others. Zero politics: nothing political is scored; the stage play The Vegetable is mentioned only as a failed attempt at a new form. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'F. Scott Fitzgerald' (https://www.britannica.com/biography/F-Scott-Fitzgerald), with the University of South Carolina Libraries' biography (https://sc.edu/about/offices_and_divisions/university_libraries/browse/irvin_dept_special_collections/collections/matthew_arlyn_bruccoli_collection_of_f_scott_fitzgerald/life_of_fitzgerald/) and Princeton University Library's Gatsby manuscript announcement as institutional statements of why he matters. READ (11 cited non-Wikidata sources: nine substantive, plus the World's Work scan and the Library of Congress record, which were used for the portrait only): Britannica; the Princeton Gatsby manuscript announcement (the library blog post and the same announcement in Princeton's news archive); the USC Libraries biography; the USC page on the MGM screenplay archive; the March 1922 Bookman essay; the CBS News report; the Library of America note; the Open Yale Courses lecture on Gatsby (the Perkins and experimentalism sections); and the University of South Carolina Press page on the Trimalchio galleys. PERSPECTIVES: university archival scholarship from Princeton and from the University of South Carolina, which both draw on Matthew Bruccoli and are treated as largely one lineage for calibration; a contemporary critic, friendly but openly critical (the 1922 essay, unsigned and attributed to Edmund Wilson); an encyclopaedia biographer (Arthur Mizener); a modern university lecturer's reading (Wai Chee Dimock); the Post's own archivist as reported by a news outlet, including Hemingway's contemporary jibe and Fitzgerald's reply only as relayed; a collaborator's testimony (Budd Schulberg) only as quoted on the USC page; and Fitzgerald's own letters only as quoted by Dimock and the USC page (self; never sole support). COUNTER-VOICES: the 1922 essay's verdict that the early work was imitative and lacked discipline and aesthetic ideas; the USC biography's note that critics were reluctant to credit him as a serious craftsman; Dimock's reading of his firmness against his editor; Hemingway's jibe about the Post as relayed by the archivist. CALIBRATION: nine rows, all resting on institutions, one biographer lineage and one contemporary critic; the highest score is 66 (aesthetic sensitivity) and the highest confidence 0.52 (persistence); no row is above 66/0.52 because the institutional sources share one scholarly lineage, the praise is largely retrospective and the contemporary critic disputed the early originality. Traits considered and not scored: discipline (output volume is documented, but the 1922 essay's lack of discipline concerns his imagination and the sources report slow progress on novels), collaboration (the Perkins relationship is described only through letters quoted by others while the one detailed collaborator dispute points the other way), conflict tolerance, curiosity, independent thinking (his stand on Gatsby's vagueness is one scholar's reading), risk tolerance and achievement drive (the sources that bear on them concern courtship, money or marriage, which are excluded), execution speed and planning orientation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): eight of nine rows were lowered before return -- perfectionism 72/0.58 to 64/0.50 (single-lineage concentration; interpretation stronger than behaviour), persistence 68/0.56 to 64/0.52 (single-biographer dependence), mastery orientation 68/0.54 to 62/0.48 and relabelled inference (admiring-source concentration), experimentation 66/0.54 to 62/0.50 (interpretation stronger than behaviour; retrospective reading), creative originality 68/0.48 to 62/0.44 (retrospective praise), aesthetic sensitivity 72/0.54 to 66/0.50 (retrospective praise), autonomy need 64/0.50 to 60/0.46 and relabelled inference (single-source dependence) and adaptability 62/0.48 to 58/0.44 (interpretation stronger than behaviour); belief updating was scored 58/0.46 from the start and not lowered. EXCLUDED: his marriage and Zelda Fitzgerald, his daughter, his drinking, health and any mental-state reading (including the passages on his 'crack-up'), his relationship with Sheilah Graham, his money troubles and spending, finances other than documented professional fees and contracts, the fact and circumstances of his death and any reading from his posthumous reputation or revival, the 1922 essay's remarks on ethnic character and personality, and Hemingway's retrospective portrait of him. DISAGREEMENTS NOTED: Princeton gives both a three-year and a four-year span and both 302 pages and just over 250 pages for the same manuscript, so the cards say 'from June 1922' and give no duration or page count; Britannica says more than 150 stories while the USC biography says some 160 magazine stories and the Post's archivist says 68 stories for the Post over 17 years, so the card says more than 150; the University of South Carolina Press says he chose a new title at Perkins's urging while Princeton says he settled on a different title after publication and that the published title was the one Perkins liked best, so no card tells the title story; Dimock's wording of the December 1924 reply was not compared with the published letters; the archivist's 68 stories and the $4,000 fee are the Post's own figures while the USC biography calls $4,000 his peak fee. NOT OPENED: Hemingway's A Moveable Feast (a retrospective, partisan account with no lawful free text found, so Hemingway appears only as relayed by the Post's archivist); the Perkins-Fitzgerald letters (Dear Scott/Dear Max) and other primary letters, Fitzgerald's Ledger, the Mizener and Bruccoli biographies, T. S. Eliot's and Mencken's 1925 comments on Gatsby, Wilson's later writings on Fitzgerald and the 2016 Fitzgerald Review article that attributes the 1922 essay, the Cambridge Edition essay 'Almost a Masterpiece' (its host was unreachable), the Princeton finding aid (blocked by bot detection), Harper's article on the 1922 essay (paywalled), Princeton's separate 'Fitzgerald in Hollywood' post (seen only through a fetch summary), and the Wikipedia article. PORTRAIT: the lead's first choice, Carl Van Vechten's 4 June 1937 portrait (Library of Congress LCCN 2004662885, reproduction number LC-USZ62-88103; a second digital record, LCCN 2004662884, is the 2,888 x 3,724 pixel file on Commons), was checked and set aside: the Library's own rights statement for the Van Vechten Photographs (last revised 7 May 2024) says the donor's restrictions expired in 1986 and that the Library 'continues to believe' the photographs are in the public domain, but it also records that the Van Vechten trustee (Logan Esdale as of 2023) has asked that the photographs not be cropped or colorized and that the photographer be credited, notes that a 1998 contact disputed the donor's executor's authority, and warns that privacy and publicity rights may apply; Van Vechten died in 1964, so this is a live trust request on an identified photographer, and a generic Commons public-domain tag does not remove it. The portrait used is the publicity photograph of Fitzgerald c. 1921, photographer unknown, distributed by his publisher Scribner's and printed in The World's Work, June 1921, page 192 (Internet Archive scan of volume 42, whose text layer has the item headed 'Scott Fitzgerald' on that page and the index entry 'Fitzgerald, Scott 192', with no photographer credit and no rights statement on the item); Wikimedia Commons file 'F Scott Fitzgerald 1921.jpg' (original 566 x 767 pixels, uploaded 13 September 2013) tags it public domain (PD-US-expired) because it was published in 1921 and cites the June 1921 magazine page and two April 1922 newspaper printings. I did not view the magazine's page image or the newspaper pages, only the scan's text layer; the Nickolas Muray 1929 portrait that Wikidata uses was not examined. The file was downloaded from Commons, opens as a 566 x 767 JPEG, and is used uncropped and not resized (never upscaled). It is classed as a likeness (a contemporary photograph of the sitter). LEAD REVIEW (Roster51): none yet.
